The LIDAR Thomson Scattering concept was first implemented on the JET tokamak in 1987.
The spatial resolution of the JET LIDAR system is around 12 cm, which corresponds to over 8% of the minor radius.
The light collection optics are located outside the biological shield, with only a few mirrors near the tokamak.
The strongest stray light source is the 'backwall pulse' when the laser hits the inner wall of the vacuum vessel.
The radial profile shape is calibrated using Raman scattering from nitrogen at a pressure of around 400 mbar.
The previously used MA-2 detectors were replaced with fast GaAsP detectors, which have a much higher average quantum efficiency.

The statistical errors in the measured electron temperature and density have been reduced by a factor of 2 or more, with errors now below 5% for temperature and 3% for density in typical plasma conditions.
The JET LIDAR diagnostic is expected to remain operational in future JET experiments, including the upcoming full-scale DT campaign.
The LIDAR concept becomes more attractive for bigger fusion devices with restricted access due to neutron radiation/activation.

The JET LIDAR diagnostic produces measurements that are in excellent agreement with other diagnostics on JET, such as the conventional High Resolution Thomson Scattering, Electron Cyclotron Emission, and Reflectometer.
The light throughput of the JET LIDAR system is limited by the narrow penetration through the concrete ceiling of the biological shield.
The spectrometer design is optimized to exclude any possible shortcut routes for the backwall stray light flash.
The absolute calibration of the density profile is achieved by cross-calibration with far-infrared interferometer measurements.
The implementation of a faster data acquisition system is pending a decision on the overvoltage protection, which would allow for a spatial resolution of around 7 cm.
The installation of a large aperture, high transmission nanowire polarizer led to a factor of 2 reduction in the plasma background light, especially for high-temperature H-mode plasmas.
